rows.stem: If \(A = kB\), where A and B are two square matrices of order n and k is a scalar, then :
rows.solution:
If \(A = kB\) then every one of the \(n\) rows of \(A\) is \(k\) times the corresponding row of \(B\). A determinant is linear in each row separately, so taking the factor \(k\) out of the first row gives one \(k\), out of the second row another, and so on — \(n\) rows give \(n\) factors. Hence

\(|A| = |kB| = k^n|B|\).

So the correct statement is \(|A| = k^n|B|\). The trap is \(|A| = k|B|\), which is the rule for multiplying a SINGLE row by \(k\), not the whole matrix; it is right only when \(n = 1\).

rows.stem: Let A and B be two matrices of suitable orders. Then, which of the following is **not** correct ?
rows.solution:
Take the four statements in turn.

\((A')' = A\) — correct: transposing twice restores the original matrix.

\((kA)' = kA'\) — correct: a scalar multiplies every entry, and transposing only moves entries about.

\((A' + B')' = A + B\) — correct: transpose distributes over addition, so \((A' + B')' = (A')' + (B')' = A + B\).

\((AB)' = A'B'\) — NOT correct. The reversal law gives \((AB)' = B'A'\), with the ORDER REVERSED. (Indeed for \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\), \((AB)' = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 11 & 23 \end{bmatrix}\) while \(A'B' = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 16 \\ 4 & 22 \end{bmatrix}\).) There is also an order reason: if \(A\) is \(m \times n\) and \(B\) is \(n \times p\), then \(A'B'\) is not even defined unless \(m = p\).

So the statement that is not correct is \((AB)' = A'B'\).

Treat \(\theta\) as a constant. Use \(\cos 2A = 2\cos^2 A - 1\) on both terms of the numerator:

\(\cos 2x - \cos 2\theta = \left(2\cos^2 x - 1\right) - \left(2\cos^2\theta - 1\right) = 2\left(\cos^2 x - \cos^2\theta\right) = 2(\cos x - \cos\theta)(\cos x + \cos\theta)\).

The factor \((\cos x - \cos\theta)\) cancels with the denominator, leaving

\(\int \frac{\cos 2x - \cos 2\theta}{\cos x - \cos\theta}\,dx = \int 2\left(\cos x + \cos\theta\right)dx = 2\left(\sin x + x\cos\theta\right) + C\),

since \(\cos\theta\) is a constant and therefore integrates to \(x\cos\theta\). So the value is \(2(\sin x + x\cos\theta) + C\). (Differentiating the choice \(2(\sin x + \sin\theta)\) gives only \(2\cos x\) — the constant term contributes nothing — so it cannot be right.)

Put \(t = 5x^2 + 1\), so \(dt = 10x\,dx\), i.e. \(2x\,dx = \frac{dt}{5}\). The limits change as \(x = 0 \Rightarrow t = 1\) and \(x = 1 \Rightarrow t = 6\). Hence

\(\int\limits_0^1 \frac{2x}{5x^2 + 1}\,dx = \frac{1}{5}\int\limits_1^6 \frac{dt}{t} = \frac{1}{5}\left[\log|t|\right]_1^6 = \frac{1}{5}\left(\log 6 - \log 1\right) = \frac{1}{5}\log 6\).

So the value of the integral is \(\frac{1}{5}\log 6\). (The \(\frac{1}{5}\) comes from the substitution and the \(6\) from the upper limit \(5(1)^2 + 1\); mixing them up gives the three distractors.)

rows.stem:
The integrating factor of the differential equation

\(\dfrac{dx}{dy} = \dfrac{-(1 + \sin x)}{x + y \cos x}\) is :
rows.solution:
The equation is written as \(\frac{dx}{dy}\), so invert it first:

\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x + y\cos x}{-(1 + \sin x)} = -\frac{x}{1 + \sin x} - \frac{y\cos x}{1 + \sin x}\).

Bringing the \(y\) term across gives the standard linear form \(\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q\):

\(\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{\cos x}{1 + \sin x}\,y = -\frac{x}{1 + \sin x}\), so \(P = \frac{\cos x}{1 + \sin x}\).

Since \(\cos x\) is exactly the derivative of \(1 + \sin x\), \(\int P\,dx = \log|1 + \sin x|\), and therefore

\(\text{I.F.} = e^{\int P\,dx} = e^{\log|1 + \sin x|} = 1 + \sin x\).

So the integrating factor is \(1 + \sin x\). It does the job it is meant to do: multiplying through by it turns the left side into \(\frac{d}{dx}\left[y(1 + \sin x)\right]\) and the equation into \(\frac{d}{dx}\left[y(1 + \sin x)\right] = -x\).

rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.solution:
\(\sin^{-1} u\) is defined only for \(-1 \le u \le 1\), so we need

\(-1 \le x^2 - 3 \le 1\).

Adding \(3\) throughout gives \(2 \le x^2 \le 4\), i.e. \(\sqrt{2} \le |x| \le 2\).

That means either \(\sqrt{2} \le x \le 2\) or \(-2 \le x \le -\sqrt{2}\).

Hence the domain is \(\left[-2, -\sqrt{2}\right] \cup \left[\sqrt{2}, 2\right]\). Both endpoints of each piece are included, since \(x^2 = 2\) gives \(x^2 - 3 = -1\) and \(x^2 = 4\) gives \(x^2 - 3 = 1\), and both are legal inputs to \(\sin^{-1}\).

rows.stem: Let the volume of a metallic hollow sphere be constant. If the inner radius increases at the rate of 2 cm/s, find the rate of increase of the outer radius when the radii are 2 cm and 4 cm respectively.
rows.solution:
Let \(R\) and \(r\) be the outer and inner radii at time \(t\). The metal in the shell has volume

\(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi\left(R^3 - r^3\right)\),

and we are told this is CONSTANT, so \(\frac{dV}{dt} = 0\). We are given \(\frac{dr}{dt} = 2\) cm/s and want \(\frac{dR}{dt}\) when \(R = 4\) cm and \(r = 2\) cm.

Differentiating with respect to \(t\),

\(\frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{4}{3}\pi\left(3R^2\,\frac{dR}{dt} - 3r^2\,\frac{dr}{dt}\right) = 0\),

so \(R^2\,\frac{dR}{dt} = r^2\,\frac{dr}{dt}\).

Substituting \(R = 4\), \(r = 2\) and \(\frac{dr}{dt} = 2\):

\(16\,\frac{dR}{dt} = 4 \times 2 = 8\), hence \(\frac{dR}{dt} = \frac{1}{2}\ \text{cm/s}\).

So the outer radius is increasing at \(\frac{1}{2}\) cm/s. (This is smaller than the inner rate, as it must be: the same amount of new inner volume is spread over a larger outer surface.)

rows.stem: Find the interval/intervals in which the function \(f(x) = \sin 3x - \cos 3x\), \(0 < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) is strictly increasing.
rows.solution:
\(f(x) = \sin 3x - \cos 3x\), so

\(f'(x) = 3\cos 3x + 3\sin 3x = 3\left(\sin 3x + \cos 3x\right)\).

For the critical points put \(f'(x) = 0\): \(\sin 3x = -\cos 3x\), i.e. \(\tan 3x = -1\). With \(0 < x < \frac{\pi}{2}\) we have \(0 < 3x < \frac{3\pi}{2}\), and the only solution of \(\tan 3x = -1\) in that range is \(3x = \frac{3\pi}{4}\), i.e. \(x = \frac{\pi}{4}\).

This single point splits \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) into two pieces. It is convenient to write \(f'(x) = 3\sqrt{2}\,\sin\left(3x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\).

For \(x \in \left(0, \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\): \(3x + \frac{\pi}{4} \in \left(\frac{\pi}{4}, \pi\right)\), where the sine is positive, so \(f'(x) > 0\).

For \(x \in \left(\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\): \(3x + \frac{\pi}{4} \in \left(\pi, \frac{7\pi}{4}\right)\), where the sine is negative, so \(f'(x) < 0\).

Hence \(f\) is strictly increasing on \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) — and only there — within the given interval.

rows.stem:
Solve the differential equation

\(x \cos\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) \dfrac{dy}{dx} = y \cos\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) + x\).
rows.solution:
Divide the whole equation by \(x\cos\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)\), which is legitimate wherever that factor is non-zero:

\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y\cos\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) + x}{x\cos\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)} = \frac{y}{x} + \sec\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)\).

The right-hand side depends on \(x\) and \(y\) only through \(\frac{y}{x}\), so the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\), giving \(\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}\):

\(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = v + \sec v \Rightarrow x\frac{dv}{dx} = \sec v\).

Separating the variables,

\(\cos v\,dv = \frac{dx}{x}\).

Integrating both sides,

\(\sin v = \log|x| + c\).

Finally substitute back \(v = \frac{y}{x}\):

\(\sin\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = \log|x| + c\),

which is the general solution (\(c\) an arbitrary constant).

rows.stem: In a rough sketch, mark the region bounded by \(y = 1 + |x + 1|\), \(x = -2\), \(x = 2\) and \(y = 0\). Using integration, find the area of the marked region.
rows.solution:
First remove the modulus. Since \(|x + 1| = x + 1\) when \(x \ge -1\) and \(|x + 1| = -(x + 1)\) when \(x \le -1\),

\(y = 1 + |x + 1| = \begin{cases} -x, & -2 \le x \le -1 \\ x + 2, & -1 \le x \le 2 \end{cases}\)

Sketch: the graph is a 'V' with its vertex at \((-1, 1)\). To the left it is the line \(y = -x\), falling from \((-2, 2)\) to \((-1, 1)\); to the right it is the line \(y = x + 2\), rising from \((-1, 1)\) to \((2, 4)\). The region to be marked is bounded above by this V, below by the x-axis \(y = 0\), and on the sides by the vertical lines \(x = -2\) and \(x = 2\). Note the whole V lies above the x-axis (its lowest point is \(y = 1\)), so the region is a single slab with no part below the axis.

Since the upper boundary changes formula at \(x = -1\), split the integral there:

\(\text{Area} = \int\limits_{-2}^{-1}(-x)\,dx + \int\limits_{-1}^{2}(x + 2)\,dx\).

First piece: \(\left[-\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_{-2}^{-1} = -\frac{1}{2} - \left(-\frac{4}{2}\right) = -\frac{1}{2} + 2 = \frac{3}{2}\).

Second piece: \(\left[\frac{x^2}{2} + 2x\right]_{-1}^{2} = (2 + 4) - \left(\frac{1}{2} - 2\right) = 6 + \frac{3}{2} = \frac{15}{2}\).

Hence \(\text{Area} = \frac{3}{2} + \frac{15}{2} = \frac{18}{2} = 9\) square units.

rows.stem: Three students run on a racing track such that their speeds add up to 6 km/h. However, double the speed of the third runner added to the speed of the first results in 7 km/h. If thrice the speed of the first runner is added to the original speeds of the other two, the result is 12 km/h. Using matrix method, find the original speed of each runner.
rows.solution:
Let the original speeds of the three runners be \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) km/h.

Translating the three statements:

the speeds add up to \(6\): \(x + y + z = 6\);

double the third added to the first gives \(7\): \(x + 2z = 7\);

thrice the first added to the ORIGINAL speeds of the other two gives \(12\): \(3x + y + z = 12\).

Write this as \(AX = B\) with

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 7 \\ 12 \end{bmatrix}\).

Expanding along the first row, \(|A| = 1(0 - 2) - 1(1 - 6) + 1(1 - 0) = -2 + 5 + 1 = 4 \ne 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists and \(X = A^{-1}B\) is the unique solution.

Computing the cofactors and transposing,

\(\operatorname{adj} A = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 & 2 \\ 5 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 & 2 \\ 5 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\).

Hence

\(\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 & 2 \\ 5 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 7 \\ 12 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix} 12 \\ 4 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

So the original speeds are \(3\) km/h, \(1\) km/h and \(2\) km/h respectively.

Check: \(3 + 1 + 2 = 6\); \(3 + 2(2) = 7\); \(3(3) + 1 + 2 = 12\) — all three conditions hold.
